conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time for this today. I’m Dr. Lee, a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers with emotional health after delivery.  

I’d like to use a brief questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short—to understand how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days. It’s simply a way to make sure we’re not missing anything that might be making motherhood harder than it has to be.  

Everything we discuss stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, and you can skip any question you’d rather not answer. We’ll go through ten questions, and I’ll ask each one conversationally—no need to remember numbers or categories.  

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:  

In the past week, when you were able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how did that feel for you?

Honestly? Laughing feels… kind of distant. I can chuckle if my husband makes a joke or if the baby does something silly, but the sound feels flat, like I’m just pretending. I’ll smile, yet the happy feeling doesn’t really reach me the way it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly it feels forced. I’ll catch myself smiling at something small the baby does, but the laughter fades fast and I’m right back to feeling empty or worried.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just watching a show I liked—but now it all feels like one more thing I have to get through. I’ll think “I should be looking forward to this,” but mostly I’m just tired and hoping I can fake my way through it without falling apart.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… almost every day. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe my milk isn’t enough or I missed his cues. I lie in bed replaying every little thing: the diaper change that took too long, the moment I looked at my phone instead of him. My head tells me other moms would handle it better, and the guilt just sits on my chest like a weight.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes—pretty much all the time. My mind keeps spinning with “what-ifs” about the baby: Is he breathing? Is that rash normal? Am I missing something that could hurt him? There’s no real reason, but the worry just parks itself in my chest and won’t leave.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s not every day, but a couple of times this week I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing and I feel like I can’t get a full breath. Nothing’s happening—no noise, no sudden movement—but it’s like my body decides we’re in danger and I have to check the locks, check the baby, check everything. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the second I finish one thing—feeding, changing, trying to get him to nap—there’s another pile of laundry or dishes or a text I forgot to answer. I keep thinking, “I should be able to handle this; people do it every day,” but the list never shrinks and I end up frozen, just staring at it while my chest gets tight.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. After the night feeds I’ll lie there staring at the ceiling, running through every little thing I might have done wrong or worrying something will happen to him. Even when he’s sleeping soundly, my mind won’t shut off. I finally drift off maybe two hours before he wakes again, then I feel guilty for being tired.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s a gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be changing his diaper and suddenly feel like crying for no reason, or I’ll watch other moms on social media looking so happy and think, “Why can’t I feel that way?” I keep telling myself I should be grateful, but the sadness just sits there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened three or four times since last weekend. Yesterday I was rocking him and started tearing up because I felt like he deserved a mom who wasn’t so weepy. I try to keep it quiet so my husband won’t worry, but the tears just come and I can’t stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel like me again so I can be the mom he needs.

You've shared that the joy you once found in small moments now feels distant and forced, replaced by a heavy cloud of sadness, constant worry, and exhaustion that follows you through each day. Despite loving your baby deeply, you carry relentless guilt and self-criticism, replaying ordinary caregiving moments as personal failures, while panic episodes and sleepless nights leave you feeling overwhelmed and "frozen." Your honesty about frequent tears, near-daily anhedonia, and the sense that your laughter no longer reaches your heart highlights the emotional weight you're bravely carrying in this postpartum period.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient acknowledges only brief, fleeting moments of amusement that quickly give way to emptiness and worry, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory joy, describing activities as burdensome and herself as merely "faking" her way through them.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "almost every day" and gives multiple detailed examples, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant, intrusive worries without real cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden episodes of racing heart, breathlessness, and urge to check surroundings that occur "a couple of times this week," aligning with "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>She reports difficulty coping "most days" and feeling frozen, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sleep difficulty "most of the time" with prolonged nighttime rumination and near-nightly pattern.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness, spontaneous tearfulness, and persistent low mood matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes in one week, actively hiding them, consistent with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 23 places you well above the EPDS cutoff of 12-13 that flags high probability of <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. You endorse core depressive symptoms (daily sadness, crying, loss of interest) and anxiety symptoms (constant worry, two panic-like episodes, physical tension) persisting most days for the past week, alongside guilt, self-blame, and functional impairment consistent with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>. Absence of self-harm ideation is noted, yet severity warrants immediate clinical evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Request formal assessment for <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med> and possible <med>anxiety disorders</med>
3. Discuss evidence-based treatment options including <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, and medication compatible with breastfeeding if indicated
4. Coordinate practical help-partner, family, or postpartum doula support for household tasks and infant care so you can rest
5. Practice gentle sleep hygiene: short wind-down routine, limit screens after night feeds, brief mindfulness or breathing exercise
6. Schedule EPDS re-screen in 1-2 weeks to monitor progress
7. If distress escalates or thoughts of self-harm emerge, seek emergency care or call 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)-style questionnaire, 10 items, self-report.

Symptoms / Behaviors Reported  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, feelings of emptiness  
- Marked anhedonia (loss of interest/enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities)  
- Excessive guilt and self-blame regarding infant care  
- Intruding, distressing “what-if” worries about infant safety  
- Two panic-like episodes in past week (sudden racing heart, breathlessness, urge to check locks/infant)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia unrelated solely to infant feeding schedule  
- Daily sense of being overwhelmed, “frozen,” unable to complete routine tasks  
- Passive thoughts that infant “deserves a better mom” (no self-harm ideation endorsed)

Pattern Summary  
Responses cluster in three domains:  
1. Depressive (items 1, 2, 8, 9) – daily sadness, crying, anhedonia  
2. Anxiety (items 4, 5) – generalized worry and episodic panic  
3. Coping/self-appraisal (items 3, 6, 7) – guilt, perceived inadequacy, functional paralysis

Risk Factors Noted  
- Postpartum period (<1 yr)  
- Primiparous status implied  
- Social comparison distress (social media)  
- Absence of protective factor: restorative sleep  
- Denies suicidal or infanticidal ideation

Screening Significance  
Score pattern and qualitative detail are consistent with elevated risk for major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety in the postpartum context; warrants formal clinical interview to confirm diagnosis and determine level of care.
